newsitem.title: USA: Oil imports, aircraft behind US trade gap-Kantor.
newsitem.headline: Oil imports, aircraft behind US trade gap-Kantor.

text.p: U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor said Wednesday that rising prices on oil imports and a temporary drop in aircraft exports were behind an increase in the U.S. trade gap in September.

"The trade deficit increased in September, partly due to rising oil prices and partly to a temporary decline in aircraft shipments," Kantor told reporters following a Commerce Department report showing a 10.1 percent increase in the monthly trade gap in September.
Kantor said higher oil prices would continue to have an impact on monthly U.S. trade data.

"Oil prices have been going up and they have gone up again in October," Kantor said. "Therefore, even based on the same volumes, we would have a larger deficit in oil in the month of October. It has a rather profound effect on our trade situation."
The price of imported crude oil rose to an average $20.02 per barrel in September from $18.65 per barrel in August, the Commerce Department said in its monthly trade report.
The volume crude oil imports rose to an average eight million barrels per day in September, from 7.4 million barrels in August, the department said.
Kantor noted that U.S. exports of capital and consumer goods as well as services were doing well.
Kantor also said that sluggish economies of Europe, Canada and Japan have hurt U.S. trade and said that slowing economic growth among other Asian countries has also taken a toll on U.S. exports.
He said the U.S. trade deficit with Asian nations outside of Japan and China rose by $1 billion in September.

"That is due mainly to a slowdown in those economies, so we can see the profound effect a slowdown in economies has on a trade situation," Kantor said. He said trade with Asian countries outside of Japan and China grew by 24 percent last year but is only growing by a 3.4 percent rate this year.
Kantor also noted that the growth in the bilateral trade gap with China has slowed, but added that there was still much work to be done in opening China's markets despite some progress on that front.

"The size of the trade gap with China demonstrates that we must continue to assign great importance to our discussions with the Chinese and that they must live up to their international trade obligations," Kantor said.
